title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and often trailing asterisks for bold formatting) that begins an item in an enumerated list, such as '2.', '3.', '4.' or '5.' at the start of a list entry, frequently followed by markdown bold markers. It activates specifically on the list-marker token itself rather than on the content of the item, appearing across many different topics (advice lists, strategies, relationship tips, financial guidance) as long as the text is structured as a sequence of numbered steps or points. It does not activate on ordinary prose sentences that lack list formatting, on introductory sentences that merely precede a list (e.g. 'Here are some strategies:'), or on narrative/advisory sentences without a leading enumerator, even if they share similar advice-giving content.

title: Bolded list-item advice header
description: This latent fires on individual bullet/numbered list entries that give concrete, actionable suggestions, especially those formatted as a short bolded label followed by a colon and an imperative elaboration (e.g. "Attend events**: Look for local meetups..."). It activates most strongly on items from how-to/self-help/listicle style text covering hobbies, career, wellness, cooking, socializing, etc., where each line proposes a distinct concrete step or option. It activates more weakly but still fires on plain imperative advice sentences within similar advice-giving lists that lack the bolded-header formatting. It would not activate on narrative, explanatory, or emotionally validating prose that isn't structured as a discrete actionable suggestion (e.g. reassurance, analysis of someone's feelings, or general statements without a directive/action framing).

title: Empathetic exclamatory framing
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases that emotionally validate or frame the user's situation before (or instead of) substantive content — e.g. "What a great question!", "What a tricky situation!", "The age-old dilemma!", "I feel you!", "I totally understand!". These are stock conversational openers/reactions used by an assistant persona (often advice-giving, e.g. AITA-style responses) to acknowledge, sympathize with, or dramatize the topic in a punchy, exclamation-marked way, frequently just a noun phrase or short sentence standing alone. It activates most strongly on the purest, most template-like instances of this pattern (bare exclamations like "The drama!" or "Not at all!") and less strongly when similar validating sentiment is embedded in longer, more discursive sentences. It would not activate on neutral descriptive statements, detailed explanations, verdicts/judgments (e.g. "You are not the asshole"), or empathetic statements that are phrased as full explanatory sentences rather than short exclamatory framings.

title: Clarifying follow-up questions (chatbot probing style)
description: This latent fires on open-ended, clarifying questions—often in a therapeutic, coaching, or advice-chatbot register—that probe for more detail about a feeling, situation, person, or motivation the user has just mentioned, frequently offering a list of possible options ('Is it X, Y, or something else?') or asking about patterns, timing, and specifics. It activates most strongly on short, standalone interrogative or list-style prompts (e.g., 'Is it a specific incident or a pattern of behavior?', 'What are your goals and aspirations?', 'Is it the location, the people, or something else?') that function as diagnostic or reflective prompts inviting elaboration rather than asserting content. It does not activate on declarative statements, factual explanations, instructions without a question form, or narrative/descriptive text that doesn't invite the reader to specify or reflect on their own situation—so a sentence describing an event or giving a direct answer would not trigger it, even if topically similar.

title: List-introducing transition phrase
description: This latent fires on short formulaic transition phrases that introduce an upcoming enumerated list or explanation, such as 'Here's why:', 'Here are some points to consider:', 'Here are a few suggestions:', immediately followed by a numbered list marker (e.g. '1.'). It activates most strongly on the bare colon-terminated lead-in itself, especially generic templates like 'Here's why', 'Here are some [points/tips/suggestions/reasons] to consider', regardless of the topic that follows. It activates more weakly on similar sentences embedded in longer surrounding context or on structurally similar but non-listy transitions (e.g. rhetorical questions, verdict statements, or advice given in prose without a following numbered list), and does not activate on the substantive content of the list items themselves or on sentences that merely discuss advice-giving without this specific 'here's X:' + list-marker syntactic pattern.

title: Actionable self-help advice items
description: This latent fires on short, imperative or bullet-point style recommendations from advice-genre text (career, finance, relationships, health, hobbies, self-improvement), especially list items that suggest a concrete action, resource, or step the reader can take, often bolded as a mini-heading followed by elaboration (e.g., 'Network and collaborate:', 'Check and replace air filters:', 'Start small:'). It activates on sentences offering practical suggestions, tips, or options ('You can use...', 'Consider...', 'Try...', 'Look into...') as well as fragments/headers that introduce such tips. It does NOT activate strongly on purely narrative, emotional-validation, or abstract reflective statements that lack an actionable or list-like advice structure (e.g., general reassurances like 'It's not your fault' or descriptive facts without a suggested action), though some overlap with emotional-support phrasing occurs when it's embedded in an advice list.

title: Advice to communicate and resolve conflict
description: This latent fires on advice-giving language that recommends open, calm, empathetic communication as the means to resolve interpersonal conflict—phrases like 'communication is key,' 'have an open and honest conversation,' 'find common ground/compromise,' or 'approach with empathy and understanding.' It activates on sentences that prescribe a relational-repair strategy (talking it out, listening, compromising, rebuilding trust) typically in advice-column or counseling-style responses about relationships, roommates, partners, family, or coworkers. It does not activate on sentences that merely describe a conflict, state facts, give unrelated procedural instructions, or offer advice unrelated to interpersonal dialogue/empathy (e.g., financial tips, technical steps, or purely descriptive statements without a communication/resolution framing).

title: Reassuring second-person affirmation
description: This latent fires on empathetic, direct-address statements that reassure the reader of their worth, validity, or right to prioritize their own well-being, typically phrased as 'You are...' or 'Remember, you...' constructions. It activates most strongly on formulaic affirmations combining 'you deserve/are/have the right to' with themes of self-care, mental health, not being alone, and being treated with kindness or respect — the kind of closing encouragement found in advice or therapeutic-style responses. It does not activate on neutral second-person statements that give factual information, instructions, or advice about relationships/situations without an affirming, validating emotional tone (e.g., statements about compromise, boundaries-setting mechanics, or logistical suggestions), even if they share topical overlap with self-care or relationships; the key trigger is the reassuring, validating rhetorical stance directed at 'you,' not merely the topic of well-being.

title: Validating and reframing statements in advice-giving
description: This latent fires on second-person, advice-column-style sentences that validate, reassure, or reframe the reader's feelings and actions -- e.g. 'You're not the asshole,' 'It's understandable that...,' 'You didn't do anything wrong by...' It captures the rhetorical move of legitimizing someone's emotions or behavior, often by explicitly naming them as reasonable, natural, valid, or not their fault, frequently paired with a 'but/however' pivot that introduces nuance or a competing perspective. It activates most strongly on direct second-person judgments about blame, fault, or emotional validity within an interpersonal conflict narrative (classic 'am I the asshole' or relationship-advice framing). It would not activate on neutral factual statements, third-person narration without evaluative framing, or purely descriptive/procedural text lacking any judgment about whether someone's feelings or actions are justified.

title: Interpersonal validation and advice-giving stance
description: This latent fires on sentences in an advice-giving or supportive-counselor register that validate the reader's feelings, assign or absolve responsibility ('you're not obligated to...', 'that's not okay/healthy'), or normalize others' possible motives ('they may not have meant...', 'it's understandable that...'). It activates on evaluative judgments about relationships, boundaries, and behavior (e.g., labeling something as unhealthy, disrespectful, or reasonable) and on reassuring, empathetic framing typical of relationship/advice-column text. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, technical explanations, or narrative descriptions lacking this second-person or relational-judgment framing, even if they share topical overlap with relationships or emotions.
